passage:
Simran, come sit. Your Maria Aunty wasn't always calm about this sort of thing. In Class 9 there was a boy, Dinesh, who took my lunch and laughed at my glasses. I was terrified to tell anyone, because I was sure he would find me after school. For a month I said nothing, and my stomach hurt every morning.
Then our school put a complaint box outside the office, no name needed. I dropped in a note with the dates. I walked to the gate with two friends for weeks, never alone. And I let the principal and my parents deal with him. I never faced him myself.
My fear was reasonable, Simran. It never meant I shouldn't tell.

qa.q: What did the school put outside the office?
qa.a: The school put a complaint box outside the office, where no name was needed.

qa.q: Why did Maria stay silent for a month?
qa.a: She was terrified that Dinesh would find her after school, so she was afraid of what he would do if she spoke.

qa.q: What could Simran do if afraid a bully will get back at them?
qa.a: Simran can use an anonymous route like the box, stay with friends instead of alone, and let adults handle the danger.

qa.q: How might the principal have seen the note in the box?
qa.a: The principal probably saw it as a chance to learn about the problem and act on it without exposing the student who wrote it.

grounding: An elder recalls fear of a bully's retaliation and how an anonymous note, staying in a group and letting adults act kept her safe.

passage:
Dear Indu didi,
You asked how school is. Something happened yesterday and I keep thinking about it. In Hindi class Rohan started doing an impression of Chirag's stutter, and half the class laughed. Chirag stared at his desk. My heart was thumping so hard I could feel it in my ears.
I put my hand up. I didn't shout. I said, "That's not funny, Rohan. Please stop." It went quiet for a second. Then Ms. Pillai said, "Thank you, Vaibhav. Rohan?" and Rohan muttered sorry.
Afterwards Chirag didn't say anything, but he moved his bag so I could sit beside him. I was still shaking a bit, but I'm glad.
Write back soon.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Whose stutter did Rohan imitate in Hindi class?
qa.a: Rohan imitated Chirag's stutter.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling before putting a hand up?
qa.a: Vaibhav was scared, with a heart thumping so hard it could be felt in the ears, but was still determined to speak.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do if Rohan makes the joke again?
qa.a: Vaibhav can stay calm and say again that it is not funny, and tell Ms. Pillai if it continues.

qa.q: How might Chirag have felt during and after the joke?
qa.a: Chirag was probably humiliated, since he stared at his desk, and then supported when he moved his bag so Vaibhav could sit beside him.

grounding: A teen quietly and calmly speaks up in class against a joke that humiliates a classmate, showing that small stands change what is normal.

passage:
There was a folded note on my desk on Monday morning. Seema, in her tiny handwriting: "Thanks for saying something on Friday." That's all. She didn't look at me all day, and I didn't look at her, but I think we both knew.
The funny part is that all I said to the boys at the gate was, "Leave her alone, it's not that deep." My voice wobbled. I honestly thought it barely counted. But Seema told me later that what stayed with her was that somebody turned around and saw her.
I'm Leela, and what I learned is that you don't need a big speech. Sometimes being seen matters more. So I said, "You're welcome." That was enough.

qa.q: What did Seema write on the folded note?
qa.a: She wrote, "Thanks for saying something on Friday."

qa.q: What did Leela think of the words Leela said at the gate?
qa.a: Leela thought they barely counted, because Leela's voice wobbled and all Leela said was 'Leave her alone, it's not that deep'.

qa.q: What can someone in Leela's place take from Seema's thanks?
qa.a: They can accept thanks simply and know that a small stand, and being seen, can matter more than any speech.

qa.q: What stayed with Seema most, according to Leela?
qa.a: What stayed with Seema was that somebody turned around and saw her.

grounding: A defended student thanks the defender quietly, and the defender learns that being seen can matter more than any speech.

passage:
I'm Joseph. In November some boys in my class passed around a photo of Reena tripping on the stairs, with a mean caption. I saw it on my phone and did nothing. I didn't laugh and I didn't share, but I didn't speak either. Reena stayed away from school for two days. When she came back, her eyes were red.
I felt sick. I kept telling myself I hadn't done anything, which was exactly the problem.
So I found her at the library door. "I saw that photo and I stayed quiet. I'm sorry. I should have said something." She looked at me for a moment and said, "Thanks for saying it." I have also told our class teacher what I knew. Next time I'll speak sooner.

qa.q: Where did Joseph find Reena to apologise?
qa.a: Joseph found Reena at the library door.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel sick?
qa.a: Joseph realised that saying "I hadn't done anything" was exactly the problem: the silence had let Reena be hurt, and Joseph felt guilty.

qa.q: What could Joseph do next time he sees something like this?
qa.a: Joseph could speak up sooner, saying it isn't okay or telling a teacher, and can keep checking that Reena is alright.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when she came back to school?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and embarrassed, since her eyes were red, so Joseph's apology may have meant a lot to her.

grounding: A teen who stayed quiet while a classmate was hurt feels guilt, apologises, tells the teacher and resolves to speak sooner.

passage:
At 9:40 on the last night before the project deadline, Tarun opened his sent-mail folder and his stomach dropped: he had emailed Mr. Sarkar last term's file, not this one. The portal closed at ten. Load-shedding had already stopped the fan, and the room was hot and dim.
You idiot, he thought. Useless. You can't even attach a file. He typed "I'm stupid" into his notes and stared at the words.
The phone buzzed. Anand: "Bro, done?" Tarun told him.
"If I had done this, what would you say to me?" Anand asked.
Tarun paused. "That everyone does it. Send the right one now."
"So?"
Tarun attached the correct file, added a line of apology, and pressed send at 9:52.

qa.q: At what time did Tarun press send on the correct file?
qa.a: He pressed send at 9:52.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he typed "I'm stupid"?
qa.a: He was panicking and attacking himself, calling himself an idiot and useless over one wrong attachment.

qa.q: What helped Tarun move from self-attack to action?
qa.a: Anand's question about what Tarun would say to a friend made Tarun hear his own kinder answer, and he then fixed the problem.

qa.q: How does Anand see Tarun's mistake?
qa.a: Anand treats it as something anyone could do, and Anand's question suggests Anand does not see Tarun as useless.

grounding: After a mistake a teen calls himself stupid and useless; asking what he would tell a friend softens the cruel voice and lets him fix the problem.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, and I was working the stall next to Sabina's at the school fete. She was carrying a tray of twenty cups of tea across the tent when her foot caught a rope, and everything went down. Tea, glass, silence. Everyone looked.
Sabina winced and said quietly, "Ouch. That one's on me." She stood still for a second with her hand on her chest, breathed out, and then said, "Right. Broom. Then round two." I brought the dustpan. She laughed a little, but her hands were shaking as she swept.
I don't know what was going on inside her. Maybe she was mortified. But she didn't call herself names, and the second tray reached the table ten minutes later without a single cup lost.

qa.q: What did Sabina's foot catch on?
qa.a: Her foot caught on a rope.

qa.q: What might Sabina have been feeling after the tray fell, according to Bhupen?
qa.a: She may have felt stung or mortified, since she winced, held her chest and her hands shook, though Bhupen admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: How could someone copy Sabina's way of handling a mistake?
qa.a: They can own it, feel the sting, and take the next practical step, like the broom and round two, without calling themselves names.

qa.q: How does Bhupen read Sabina's reaction?
qa.a: Bhupen is unsure what she felt inside, but notices that she did not call herself names and that she fixed the mess kindly and quickly.

grounding: An observer sees Sabina own a mistake, feel the sting and treat herself kindly enough to fix it.

passage:
Parul, stop hiding your face, I'm not going to scold you. Let me tell you about your Vasudha Aunty at sixteen. I was in charge of sending our team's entry form for the inter-school quiz, and I forgot. The date passed. Four of us had studied for months. When I told them, I felt lower than the floor.
My friend Neha didn't shout. She sat next to me on the steps and said, "Everyone messes up. Even the teacher forgot the bell yesterday." Then she simply stayed there, eating her chikki, while I cried.
A weight lifted, beta. Not all of it, but enough for me to think again. The next year I set a reminder and sent the form early. And I try to be a Neha to others.

qa.q: What did Vasudha forget to send?
qa.a: She forgot to send her team's entry form for the inter-school quiz.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when she told her team?
qa.a: She felt lower than the floor, since four of them had studied for months and the date had passed.

qa.q: What can Parul do when a friend makes a mistake?
qa.a: Parul can be like Neha: stay beside the friend, say that everyone messes up, and help think about what to do next.

qa.q: How might Neha have seen Vasudha's mistake?
qa.a: Neha saw it as an ordinary slip that everyone makes, and chose to stay rather than to scold.

grounding: An elder recalls a friend who said everyone messes up and stayed with her after a serious mistake, and how it lifted the weight.

passage:
Sunday. Suraj's father set the tuition attendance sheet on the table: four weeks of blank boxes. Suraj had said he was going and had spent the evenings at the cyber cafe instead. "I'm very disappointed," his father said, and went out to the balcony. Suraj lay awake thinking, I'm worthless, I ruin everything.
Tuesday. He told his friend Wasim. "What you did was wrong," Wasim said, "but that doesn't make you worthless." That evening Suraj wrote a note: he apologised, promised to attend every class, and asked his father to check the sheet each week.
The following Sunday his father read the note twice. "Trust comes back slowly," he said. "But show me." Suraj nodded and packed his tuition bag.

qa.q: How many weeks of blank boxes were on the attendance sheet?
qa.a: There were four weeks of blank boxes.

qa.q: What was Suraj thinking on Sunday night?
qa.a: He was thinking he was worthless and ruined everything, because his father's disappointment felt like a verdict on him.

qa.q: What did Suraj do to repair the situation?
qa.a: He apologised in a note, promised to attend every class and asked his father to check the sheet each week, which separates his act from his worth.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father have been feeling?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and disappointed by the lie, since he went out to the balcony, yet he was still willing to rebuild trust slowly.

grounding: A parent is upset after a serious mistake and the teen feels worthless, then separates his act from himself, apologises and repairs, over three days.

passage:
Dear Seema Masi,
I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. For the past few days everything has felt pointless. I wake up already tired. I keep going over the mistake I made in the exam, and I am so angry at myself that I can hardly look in the mirror. It hasn't stopped for days. I don't think anyone would understand.
But I know you would listen. I don't want to keep this to myself any more. Could you come with me to see the school counsellor on Monday? I'm scared to go alone. And if the feelings ever get frightening and I feel unsafe, I will call the helpline number printed in my school diary right away.
Thank you for reading this.
Leela

Under it, in Masi's handwriting that evening: "Leela, I'm here now, downstairs. We'll talk tonight and I'll stay till you sleep. One exam doesn't change how loved you are. Monday, we go together."

qa.q: Who does Leela ask to come along to the school counsellor?
qa.a: Leela asks Seema Masi to come along.

qa.q: Why is Leela writing a letter instead of speaking?
qa.a: Leela feels scared and alone, sure no one would understand, so writing is easier than speaking; Leela trusts Seema Masi to listen.

qa.q: What should Leela do if the feelings become frightening?
qa.a: Leela should call the helpline number in the school diary right away and tell a trusted adult, as the letter promises.

qa.q: How does Seema Masi respond to the letter?
qa.a: Seema Masi comes that same evening, promises to stay and talk until Leela sleeps, says Leela is still loved, and will go along on Monday.

grounding: A teen who feels everything is pointless and is very angry at themself reaches out in a letter to a trusted adult and plans to see a counsellor and use a helpline if unsafe.

passage:
In the kasba school at the foot of the hills, Ayesha's Hindi essay came back with a red mark on one word and a note: "Very good." She read only the red mark. That night under the bulb she copied the whole essay again, twice, until her wrist ached and her eyes burned. When she was done she tore up both attempts.
Keerthana Ma'am found her before assembly, hollow-eyed. "The essay was very good, Ayesha. Why the rewriting?"
"One word was wrong."
"One word. Next time fix that word and move on. Try to be a little better than last month, not flawless." She handed the essay back. "Pick one small thing to improve this week."
Ayesha chose spelling, and slowly put the essay in her bag.

qa.q: What did Ayesha's Hindi essay get on one word?
qa.a: It got a red mark on one word.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha copy the essay out again and again?
qa.a: She could not accept anything short of perfect: she read only the red mark and ignored the 'Very good'.

qa.q: What small step did Keerthana Ma'am suggest?
qa.a: She suggested picking one small thing to improve this week and aiming to be a little better than last month, not flawless.

qa.q: How does Keerthana Ma'am see the essay and Ayesha's rewriting?
qa.a: She sees the essay as very good and the rewriting as unnecessary, and the hollow eyes tell her that Ayesha is punishing herself.

grounding: A girl in a small town punishes herself for one small error; a teacher suggests aiming for improvement and one small step, not perfection.
